title: The Super El Niño Won't Fix the West's Water Crisis
gist: Lakes Mead and Powell have hit record lows and the Colorado River's century-old water-rights compact expires at the end of 2026, and climate scientists say even the strongest El Niño on record won't meaningfully reverse the crisis because its rain mostly falls on the wrong (Lower Basin) states and climate change has permanently altered how precipitation converts to reservoir supply.

insights.claim: The Colorado River supplies water to 40 million people across seven states, and its two largest reservoirs, Lakes Mead and Powell, have each hit multiple record low points this month.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Establishes the scale of population and reservoir stress underlying the crisis, relevant to utilities, agriculture, and municipal water planners across the Southwest.
insights.locator: The Colorado River, which provides water for 40 million people

insights.claim: As of the reporting date, Lake Powell sat at 3,519.4 feet and Lake Mead at 1,039.6 feet, their lowest levels on record; both reservoirs hit a 'deadpool' threshold (3,370 feet for Powell, 895 feet for Mead) below which water can no longer flow downstream, with hydropower generation affected or offline even earlier.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Quantifies concrete, trackable thresholds at which downstream water delivery and hydropower generation would fail entirely, a hard operational risk line for the region's power and water supply.
insights.locator: On Thursday, Lake Powell was sitting at 3,519.4 feet

insights.claim: A century-old compact governing Colorado River water rights expires at the end of 2026, and states have already missed several deadlines to negotiate a replacement, forcing the federal government to step in.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A hard regulatory deadline colliding with record-low reservoirs creates a near-term political/legal catalyst that could reallocate water rights across agriculture, cities, and industry in the Southwest.
insights.locator: A century-old compact dictating water rights from the river runs out at the end of this year

insights.claim: The Colorado River's water has for decades been over-allocated to water-intensive industries such as agriculture, a structural root cause of the current supply-demand gap.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Identifies agricultural over-allocation, not just drought, as a core structural driver — meaning demand-side reform, not just weather, is required to resolve the crisis.
insights.locator: the river, whose water has for decades been over-allocated to thirsty industries like agriculture

insights.claim: Western Resource Advocates policy manager John Berggren says the long-anticipated Colorado River crisis has now arrived, with observers repeatedly saying 'this is the year' as conditions worsen.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: An expert on-the-ground assessment that the crisis has shifted from a long-term projection to an active, present emergency.
insights.quote: People have talked about the Colorado River crisis for decades—we're now in it.
insights.locator: says John Berggren, a policy manager at environmental nonprofit Western Resource Advocates

themes.theme: Why El Niño won't fix it

insights.claim: This year's El Niño is shaping up to be the strongest on record and is expected to bring increased rain and snowfall to the Southwest, but experts caution the increased precipitation won't be enough to resolve the Colorado River's longer-term structural problems.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Pushes back on a naive 'strong El Niño will fix the drought' narrative, important for anyone modeling water-supply recovery timelines in the Southwest.
insights.locator: The weather phenomenon, which is shaping up to be the strongest one of its kind in recorded history

insights.claim: A strong El Niño reliably brings wet weather to Lower Basin states (Southern California through Arizona, New Mexico, and the Gulf Coast) but has only a modest, unreliable correlation with snowpack in the Upper Basin states (Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, Wyoming) whose snowmelt is what actually replenishes Lakes Powell and Mead.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A key mechanistic nuance: even a historic El Niño may deliver rain to the 'wrong' states and do little to refill the reservoirs that matter most, undercutting optimistic near-term supply forecasts.
insights.quote: A strong El Niño does load the dice toward a wet winter across the southern US, from Southern California through Arizona and New Mexico to the Gulf Coast.
insights.locator: Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather says

insights.claim: During the last very strong El Niño (winter 2015-16), the Upper Basin experienced only a 'normal' amount of snowfall, and peer-reviewed correlations between El Niño and Upper Basin snowpack or streamflow are described as modest at best.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Historical precedent directly undercuts hopes that this El Niño will meaningfully replenish the reservoirs feeding the Lower Basin.
insights.quote: Peer-reviewed correlations between El Niño and Upper Basin snowpack or streamflow are modest at best.
insights.locator: Hausfather points out that during the last "very strong" El Niño

insights.claim: Because this El Niño is unusually strong ('ridiculously strong'), climate scientist Daniel Swain says there's a chance some of its precipitation could still reach the Upper Basin states, unlike in typical El Niño years.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A narrow, uncertain upside case that this specific extreme El Niño could behave differently from historical norms and partially replenish the critical reservoirs.
insights.locator: there's a chance that some of the Upper Basin states could see some of that precipitation

insights.claim: Climate change has raised the baseline temperature of Western winters, making 'snow droughts' more common, and even when precipitation increases, it is more likely to be absorbed by dry soil, re-evaporated into a thirstier atmosphere, or fall as rain rather than snow, so it no longer replenishes reservoirs the way a comparable wet year did in the 1980s or 1990s.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A key mechanism showing that historical rainfall-to-reservoir conversion rates no longer apply, meaning even 'good' precipitation years deliver less real water supply than they used to.
insights.quote: That won't have the same effect as a good snow year in 1980 or 1990.
insights.locator: Precipitation can be "intercepted by drying soil

insights.claim: Some projections show the Colorado River's flow could shrink by as much as 30 percent by 2050 due to climate change.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A concrete long-term supply-decline figure relevant to any long-horizon planning for Southwest water, agriculture, or power markets.
insights.locator: Some projections show that the river's flow could shrink as much as 30 percent by 2050

insights.claim: All experts cited agree that even a best-case, record snowpack year would only provide temporary relief, not solve the underlying structural water crisis.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Sets expectations that no single favorable weather year changes the trajectory; durable fixes require policy/allocation reform, not weather luck.
insights.quote: Even one big year is not going to save us. It might be a sigh of relief, but we'll be right back in it.
insights.locator: "Even one big year is not going to save us," says Beggren
